justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a mild upward drift from what I assessed as the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the recent closing price and applied only a small positive adjustment, reflecting the tendency of asset prices to exhibit short-term momentum while also mean-reverting around recent levels. The one-week estimate nudged slightly higher, incorporating the assumption that any near-term catalyst or broader market trend would carry prices modestly forward. The one-month estimate continued this gentle upward trajectory, consistent with a long-run drift assumption embedded in equity-like assets, though the increment was deliberately conservative given the many things that can shift over a month.

The confidence interval widths reflect the natural scaling of uncertainty with time. At one day, realized volatility is relatively constrained, so my interval was tight — roughly plus or minus 12 points around the point estimate. By one week, uncertainty compounds as new information can arrive across multiple trading sessions, widening the interval to about 22 points on each side. At one month, the interval expands further to roughly 40 points in each direction, capturing the accumulated effect of earnings announcements, macroeconomic data releases, and shifts in market sentiment that become increasingly unpredictable over that horizon.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic conditions — such as a surprise inflation print, an unexpected Federal Reserve policy shift, or a geopolitical shock — could drive prices well below my lower bounds. Liquidity crunches or correlated selling across asset classes could amplify any initial move. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected earnings season, a dovish pivot from central banks, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical tension could push prices meaningfully above my upper bounds.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals are calibrated under roughly normal market conditions. Fat-tail events — low-probability but high-impact occurrences such as a financial institution failure, a sudden credit market dislocation, or an unexpected geopolitical escalation — are by their nature underrepresented in historical volatility estimates. These events could produce moves that dwarf my stated confidence intervals, particularly at the one-month horizon where there is simply more time for rare events to materialize.
